comment: Geography (AQA GCSE 8035) multiple choice — Paper 1 Section B (The living world: ecosystems, tropical rainforests, cold environments) and Section C (Physical landscapes in the UK: coastal and glacial). Definitions in AQA's own wording from the school's List of Key Terms, case study figures from the Dulwich Case Study Summary Booklet 2026 (Amazon, Svalbard, Dorset, Brighton, Lake District), processes from the topic revision mats, and the errors the school's own feedback lesson and the mark schemes flag. Four options; answer is the 0-based index of the correct one.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: AQA defines an ecosystem as…
options: all the animals living in one area
a community of plants and animals that interact with each other and their physical environment
a very large, naturally occurring community of flora and fauna occupying a major area
the non-living parts of an environment, such as soil, rock and climate
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Option 2 is the definition of a biome and option 3 is the definition of the abiotic components. The examined word is interact — an ecosystem is biotic and abiotic parts interacting.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Which of these is an abiotic component of a pond ecosystem?
options: Algae
Midge larvae
Heron
Dissolved oxygen
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Abiotic means relating to non-living things — the water, sunlight, dissolved oxygen, sediment and temperature. The other three are biotic.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: In the pond ecosystem John's class studied, which organism is the producer?
options: Algae
Midge larvae
Perch
Rag-tailed maggots
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Algae absorb energy from the sun by photosynthesis, so they are the energy entry point. Midge larvae are the primary consumers, perch the secondary, heron the tertiary and rag-tailed maggots the decomposers.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: In that pond ecosystem, the tertiary consumer is the…
options: midge larvae
perch
heron
algae
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Algae → midge larvae → fish such as perch → heron. The heron is at the top of the pond food chain.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: In the school's pond example, the decomposers are the…
options: herons
rag-tailed maggots
perch
midge larvae
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Rag-tailed maggots break down dead tissue so the nutrients are recycled back into the water and sediment for the algae to take up.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: AQA defines a decomposer as an organism such as a bacterium or fungus that…
options: absorbs energy from the sun through photosynthesis
eats herbivores and/or plant matter
breaks down dead tissue, which is then recycled to the environment
moves nutrients from the soil into the biomass
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Option 1 defines a producer, option 2 a consumer. The phrase worth learning is 'which is then recycled to the environment' — that is what links decomposers to the nutrient cycle.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
options: a food chain shows one line of energy flow from producer to tertiary consumer, whereas a food web shows a collection of interlinked food chains
a food chain is simply a longer version of a food web
a food web contains only plants, while a food chain contains animals too
a food chain includes decomposers and a food web does not
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: This was 2023 Q02.2, for 1 mark. The difference is structural — one line versus many interlinked lines — not a difference of size.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: In 2019 Figure 7, biomass fell from 12 000 units at the primary consumer level to 300 at the secondary consumer level. What is the percentage loss?
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: 11 700 ÷ 12 000 = 0.975, so 97.5%. This was 2019 Q02.4 — a single mark for a calculation, so practise doing it fast.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: AQA defines ecotourism as…
options: tourism in a country that has signed an international environmental agreement
responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, sustains the wellbeing of local people, and may involve education
any form of tourism that takes place outdoors
tourism that replaces logging as a country's main source of income
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The definition continues: it is usually carried out in small groups and has minimal impact on the local ecosystem. Both the small groups and the local wellbeing are mark-earning details.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The 2023 nutrient-cycle figure gave biomass stores of trunk 120, branches 80, roots 30 and leaves 10 tonnes of carbon per hectare. What percentage of the biomass is stored in the roots?
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The total is 240, and 30 ÷ 240 = 12.5%. This was 2023 Q02.6.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: According to the 2023 paper's own fact file, tropical rainforests are home to…
options: about 10% of the plant and animal species on Earth
about 25% of the plant and animal species on Earth
more than 50% of the plant and animal species on Earth
more than 90% of the plant and animal species on Earth
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The Case Study Summary Booklet puts the same point as more than two-thirds of the world's plant species and half its animal species. Either figure is creditable; both make the biodiversity-loss argument.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The three flows of the nutrient cycle are…
options: fallout, decay and uptake
runoff, leaching and weathering
biomass, litter and soil
interception, transpiration and evaporation
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Fallout moves material from biomass to litter, decay from litter to soil, and uptake from soil back to biomass. Biomass, litter and soil are the three stores, not the flows.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Why is nutrient cycling so rapid in the tropical rainforest?
options: the soil is deep and fertile, so nutrients are readily available
rainfall washes nutrients directly from the atmosphere into the biomass
the trees drop all their leaves at once, giving a single large input
high temperatures and a wet climate allow decomposers to break litter down very quickly
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The mark scheme adds that the vegetation is evergreen, so the litter layer is fed all year rather than in one autumn drop. The soil is the opposite of fertile — it is a thin, leached latosol.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The red soil found in tropical rainforests is called a…
options: podsol
latosol
chernozem
gley
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: A one-mark recall fact from the school's quick-fire list. The latosol is thin and heavily leached by the high rainfall, which is why the nutrients are held in the biomass rather than in the soil.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The UK's global ecosystem (biome) is…
options: coniferous forest
tundra
temperate deciduous forest
temperate grassland
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Another one-mark recall fact from the school's quick-fire list. Deciduous means the trees drop their leaves, which they do because of lower winter temperatures.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Which statement describes the characteristics of temperate deciduous forests?
options: the vegetation is short because the growing season only lasts two months
the trees drop their dead leaves because of lower temperatures in winter
the vegetation is sparse because rainfall is low
the vegetation is evergreen because the climate is hot all year round
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: This was 2022 Q02.3, word for word. Option 1 describes tundra, option 3 a desert and option 4 a tropical rainforest.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The three largest blocks of tropical rainforest are in…
options: Europe, Asia and Australia
North America, Europe and Asia
the Arctic, Antarctica and the Himalayas
Amazonia, central and west Africa, and south-east Asia and Indonesia
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The mark scheme for the describe-distribution question wants the Equator and the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn plus these three named blocks, with smaller areas on the north and east coasts of Australia.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Why do global ecosystems form broad belts running roughly east–west?
options: climate is controlled mainly by latitude, and lines of latitude run east–west
ocean currents all flow from east to west
the continents are themselves arranged east–west
prevailing winds blow from west to east
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Latitude controls the angle of incoming solar radiation and the global circulation of air, so the climate zones — and the ecosystems adapted to them — follow lines of latitude. Relief, ocean currents and continentality distort the pattern.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: The five layers of the tropical rainforest, from top to bottom, are…
options: canopy, emergents, shrub layer, under canopy, ground layer
emergents, canopy, under canopy, shrub layer, ground layer
ground layer, shrub layer, canopy, emergents, under canopy
emergents, under canopy, canopy, ground layer, shrub layer
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Emergents are the tallest trees that emerge from the canopy; the under canopy is mainly bare trunks and lianas; the shrub layer holds ferns and saplings; the ground layer is dark and damp with a litter layer.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: What proportion of rainforest wildlife does the canopy contain?
options: about 10%
about 25%
over 50%
over 90%
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: The school mat calls the canopy 'the sea of tree tops that contain over 50% of rainforest wildlife'. It is the figure that links the layered structure to the high biodiversity.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Temperatures in the tropical rainforest are typically…
options: above 25–35°C and almost constant all year
between 10 and 20°C with a large annual range
above 40°C in summer and below 10°C in winter
below 0°C for part of the year
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: From the Case Study Summary Booklet. The reason is latitude — the sun's energy is more concentrated near the Equator. The mark scheme explicitly rejects the idea that tropical regions are closer to the sun.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: How do drip tips help a rainforest leaf?
options: they trap water for the dry season
they reflect sunlight away from the leaf surface
they allow the leaf to absorb nutrients directly from rainwater
they allow water to run off, avoiding damage from heavy tropical rainfall
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Running the water off also stops fungi growing on a permanently wet leaf surface. Thick, waxy leaves are the separate adaptation that protects the plant from intense sunlight.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Buttress roots help a rainforest tree because…
options: they reach deep into the water table
they stop the shallowly rooted tree falling over and gather nutrients released from the litter layer into the topsoil
they store water through the dry season
they protect the trunk from being colonised by lianas
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: They are large roots on all sides of a shallowly rooted tree and deliberately do not penetrate to deeper layers, because the nutrients are in the litter layer at the surface. Option 4 is what smooth bark does.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Why do rainforest trees have thin, smooth bark?
options: it allows the trunk itself to photosynthesise
it lets the tree absorb water through the trunk
there is no cold to protect against, and smoothness stops lianas and epiphytes colonising the trunk
it makes the trunk flexible in storms
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Both halves matter — thin because there is no winter, and smooth as a defence against climbers. Lianas are vines that climb tree trunks to reach sunlight in the canopy.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: Which rainforest animal adaptation is correctly matched?
options: the gecko's large, flattened toe pads with sticky scales let it grip smooth tree trunks
the sloth excretes poison through its skin to warn predators
the jaguar's prehensile tail lets it grasp branches
the poison dart frog's thick fur keeps it camouflaged
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Poison through the skin is the poison dart frog; the prehensile tail is the spider monkey; camouflaging fur is the jaguar. The sloth has long arms, curved feet and very slow movement.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: What percentage of deforestation in the Amazon is due to cattle ranching?
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: A further 10% is due to other commercial agriculture, so around 90% of Amazon clearance is agricultural. The 2023 paper's own fact file repeats the figure as 'cattle ranching accounts for 80% of current deforestation in Brazil'.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: How long is the Trans-Amazonian Highway?
options: 400 km
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: 4000 km, and the point the Case Study Summary Booklet makes is that it 'makes the forest accessible for others to exploit' — road building is an enabling cause of deforestation. 1300 km is the Trans-Alaskan Pipeline.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: How much of the Amazon rainforest has already been destroyed?
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: From the school's quick-fire list. It is the figure that makes a conclusion decisive on any 'do you agree' question about the impacts of deforestation.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: How much carbon dioxide did tropical deforestation release between 2001 and 2019?
options: 105 gigatonnes
10.5 gigatonnes
1.05 gigatonnes
1050 gigatonnes
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: From the 2023 paper's own fact file. Use it to show the contribution to climate change is global and measured, not just 'trees absorb CO2'.

04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.q: AQA defines selective logging as…
options: removing all the trees from a small area and replanting it afterwards
logging only during the dry season
logging only hardwoods such as mahogany
the cutting out of trees which are mature or inferior, to encourage the growth of the remaining trees
04-ecosystems-and-rainforests.explain: Because the canopy and the younger trees are left standing, the litter layer and nutrient cycle survive and the soil is not exposed — which is why it counts as sustainable management.

05-cold-environments.q: A cold environment is defined as an area that…
options: experiences very low temperatures for long periods of time
is permanently covered by ice
lies inside the Arctic or Antarctic Circle
has an average annual temperature below 10°C
05-cold-environments.explain: The most extreme cold environments experience temperatures well below freezing throughout the year — Antarctica is the school's named example of an extreme cold environment.

05-cold-environments.q: Which statement is true of a polar environment but not of tundra?
options: it experiences cold temperatures
its winter months are near or in total darkness
temperatures remain below 0°C throughout the year
precipitation falls mostly as snow
05-cold-environments.explain: Both are cold and both have dark winters. The distinguishing features are that polar temperatures stay below 0°C all year and can fall below −50°C in winter, whereas tundra has a large annual range and conditions mild enough for life to thrive in summer.

05-cold-environments.q: In a polar environment, winter temperatures can fall below…
05-cold-environments.explain: The school mat gives below −50°C for polar winters. Svalbard, which is polar but maritime, reaches about −30°C, with the school's model answer quoting lows as extreme as −45°C.

05-cold-environments.q: Which feature of a climate graph most clearly identifies a tundra rather than a polar environment?
options: low total precipitation
winter months with no sunshine
temperatures below freezing in January
a large annual temperature range
05-cold-environments.explain: The mat's first point about tundra is 'there is a large annual temperature range'. Tundra also has higher precipitation than polar, especially in summer.

05-cold-environments.q: Permafrost is best defined as…
options: ground that freezes every winter and thaws every summer
hard, permanently frozen ground that is impermeable, so it prevents soil formation and acts as a barrier to water transfer
a layer of ice on the surface of tundra soil
frozen subsoil found only in Antarctica
05-cold-environments.explain: Option 1 describes the active layer, which sits above the permafrost. The impermeability is the examined detail — it is why the tundra is waterlogged in summer and why soils are so thin.

05-cold-environments.q: The active layer is…
options: the top layer of soil that freezes in winter and thaws during spring and summer
the layer of permanently frozen ground beneath the surface
the layer of vegetation covering tundra soil
the depth of soil in which decomposition takes place all year
05-cold-environments.explain: It is the only part of the soil available to plant roots, which is why tundra plants have shallow roots.

05-cold-environments.q: Why is the tundra waterlogged in summer despite its low precipitation?
options: heavy summer rainfall cannot evaporate in the cold
meltwater from glaciers floods the lowland
the impermeable permafrost beneath prevents the water draining away
the soil is rich in clay, which holds water
05-cold-environments.explain: The permafrost acts as a barrier to water transfer, so meltwater from the thawed active layer ponds on the surface, creating the lakes and wetlands of the Arctic. Low evaporation in the cold makes it worse.

05-cold-environments.q: Which statement about tundra soils is correct?
options: they are deep and highly fertile because decomposition is slow
they are deep but infertile because of leaching
they are thin but fertile because of the summer waterlogging
they are very thin and not particularly fertile, and their depth increases with distance from the poles
05-cold-environments.explain: The soils are thin because the impermeable permafrost prevents soil formation, and infertile because low temperatures make decomposition extremely slow so nutrients are released only slowly.

05-cold-environments.q: Low-growing cushion plants are adapted to the tundra because they…
options: can photosynthesise in total darkness
retain moisture and provide shelter from the drying wind
have roots that penetrate the permafrost
store water in their leaves for the winter
05-cold-environments.explain: Growing close to the ground keeps the plant below the worst of the wind, which matters because for most of the year all the water in the ground is frozen and therefore unavailable — a winter drought.

05-cold-environments.q: Why do tundra plants have shallow roots?
options: to access nutrients and water close to the surface within the active layer
because the soil below is too acidic for roots to grow
to allow the plant to be blown over without being uprooted
because deeper soil is waterlogged all year round
05-cold-environments.explain: Only the active layer thaws, so roots cannot penetrate the permanently frozen ground beneath it. The nutrients are near the surface for the same reason.

05-cold-environments.q: Mosses are well suited to the tundra because they…
options: can survive being grazed by musk oxen
have a woody stem that resists the wind
cope with waterlogged conditions in summer and survive the winter drought
fix nitrogen directly from the atmosphere
05-cold-environments.explain: Mosses can dry out and rehydrate, which is why they handle both the summer waterlogging caused by the permafrost and the winter period when all water is frozen.

05-cold-environments.q: Why do tundra flowering plants have a rapid life cycle?
options: because grazing animals eat them before they can mature
because the soil loses its nutrients within weeks
because there is 24-hour daylight, which speeds up growth
because the active layer only thaws and the light only returns for a few weeks, so they must seed within a very short summer
05-cold-environments.explain: The growing season is the binding constraint in a cold environment, so a rapid life cycle is not an advantage but the only viable strategy.

05-cold-environments.q: Which red-berry plant does the school's list name as adapted to survive in the cold?
options: marram grass
bearberry
heather
cloudberry
05-cold-environments.explain: A named species lifts an adaptations answer out of generic territory. Marram grass is the coastal sand dune pioneer, not a tundra plant.

05-cold-environments.q: Musk oxen have wide hooves because…
options: they can walk on waterlogged ground and snow
they need to dig through snow to reach lichen
they help the animal swim between islands
they spread the animal's weight on thin ice
05-cold-environments.explain: The ground is waterlogged because the impermeable permafrost prevents drainage, so an adaptation to waterlogged ground is really an adaptation to permafrost — a linkage examiners reward.

05-cold-environments.q: Why do Arctic foxes and Arctic hares turn white in winter?
options: white fur is thicker than coloured fur
it reduces heat loss by reflecting less radiation
it provides camouflage against the snow
it signals maturity to a mate
05-cold-environments.explain: Because snow cover is seasonal, the colour change rather than permanent white is what makes it effective. The thick fur on their bodies and feet is the separate adaptation, for warmth.

05-cold-environments.q: Which adaptation does the school mat give for musk oxen to keep warm?
options: a thick layer of blubber beneath the skin
fur that turns white in winter
the ability to hibernate through the polar night
two layers of fur to help insulate them
05-cold-environments.explain: Two layers trap a cushion of air next to the body, slowing heat loss dramatically at temperatures that fall below −30°C.

05-cold-environments.q: AQA defines a fragile environment as one that is…
options: home to a small number of highly specialised species
both easily disturbed and difficult to restore if disturbed
at risk from economic development
protected by international agreement
05-cold-environments.explain: The definition continues: plant communities in fragile areas have evolved in highly specialised ways to deal with challenging conditions, so they cannot tolerate environmental change. That sentence is the whole protection argument in one line.

05-cold-environments.q: AQA defines a wilderness area as…
options: a natural environment that has not been significantly modified by human activity
any area set aside by a government for conservation
an area where no people live permanently
an area whose ecosystem has been restored to its natural state
05-cold-environments.explain: The definition adds that wilderness areas are the most intact, undisturbed areas left on Earth — places humans do not control and have not developed. That is why scientists need them as an unmodified baseline.

05-cold-environments.q: Svalbard is…
options: an independent Arctic state
a Russian territory in the Barents Sea
a Norwegian territory in the Arctic Ocean
a Canadian territory north of Alaska
05-cold-environments.explain: It lies around 400 miles north of mainland Norway, has five major islands, and its capital is Longyearbyen.

05-cold-environments.q: What proportion of Svalbard's land is covered by glaciers?
options: about 10%
about 25%
about 40%
over 60%
05-cold-environments.explain: The remaining land is tundra. The figure matters because it shows the physical environment itself limits where development is possible, before any question of temperature or access.

05-cold-environments.q: What is the population of Svalbard?
05-cold-environments.explain: 2700 inhabitants — and more polar bears than people. The tiny population is what makes 400 tourism jobs and 300 mining jobs economically significant, and it is also a challenge: there is almost no local workforce.

05-cold-environments.q: How many people work in mining on Svalbard?
05-cold-environments.explain: Coal mining was historically the backbone of the economy, with Mine 7 near Longyearbyen still operating. Tourism now supports more jobs — 400 — and coal is being phased out.

05-cold-environments.q: How many tourists visit Svalbard each year?
options: 1.5 million
05-cold-environments.explain: 150 000 a year, double the 2011 figure — the doubling is as useful as the level, because it shows the trend. 45 000 of them are cruise ship passengers.

05-cold-environments.q: How many of Svalbard's annual visitors arrive as cruise ship passengers?
05-cold-environments.explain: 45 000 of the 150 000 — so about 30% arrive by sea, which concentrates visitor pressure on the short summer season and on the places cruise ships can reach.

05-cold-environments.q: How many species of fish live in the Barents Sea around Svalbard?
05-cold-environments.explain: 150 species, including commercially valuable cod and haddock. Fishing is the most reliable opportunity because, unlike tourism, it is not stopped by the polar night — but overfishing is the challenge, managed by quotas agreed with Russia.

05-cold-environments.q: How much road is there on the whole of Svalbard?
options: only 50 km
about 500 km
about 150 km
about 1300 km
05-cold-environments.explain: Only 50 km, and there is one international airport with few flights — the clearest single figure for inaccessibility, which is one of the three spec-named challenges of developing a cold environment.

05-cold-environments.q: Melting permafrost and rising sea level on Svalbard have led to…
options: 25 homes destroyed and £1.8m needed for emergency housing
2500 homes destroyed and £180m needed for emergency housing
250 homes destroyed and £18m needed for emergency housing
the capital being abandoned
05-cold-environments.explain: The drinking water in two reservoirs is also threatened and there is potential to flood the airport. These figures turn 'provision of buildings and infrastructure' from a vague challenge into a costed one.

05-cold-environments.q: How long is the Trans-Alaskan Pipeline?
options: 130 km
400 km
05-cold-environments.explain: 1300 km across the whole of Alaska. It was raised and insulated so the hot oil would not melt the permafrost, built to slide during earthquakes, and designed to stop the flow when a leak is detected — and it is still running after 20 years with no destructive oil spills.

05-cold-environments.q: Which of these is NOT a term of the Antarctic Treaty?
options: it promotes international co-operation for scientific research
it permits controlled mineral extraction by signatory states
it bans the disposal of nuclear waste
it restricts military use of the continent
05-cold-environments.explain: The Treaty has kept economic development to a minimum despite the discovery of valuable resources; it encourages controlled tourism, not controlled mining. It came into force in 1961 and is up for renegotiation in 2041, which is why the 2041 Foundation exists.

05-cold-environments.q: In June 2021 the Arctic Council agreed to…
options: prevent all unregulated fishing in Arctic waters
ban oil and gas drilling in the Arctic Ocean
cap the number of cruise ships visiting Svalbard
extend the Antarctic Treaty to the Arctic
05-cold-environments.explain: It was signed by the US, China, Russia, Canada, Japan, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, Korea and the EU. The honest weakness to include in an evaluation is that these waters are very hard to police, so the agreement relies on voluntary commitment.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: The three factors that control the size of a wave are…
options: tide, current and water depth
fetch, wind speed and wind duration
wind direction, rock type and beach gradient
swash, backwash and wave frequency
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: AQA's definition of waves builds all three in: the largest waves form where winds are very strong, blow for lengthy periods, and cross large expanses of water. Fetch is the distance the wave has travelled.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Which set of characteristics describes a destructive wave?
options: low height, long wavelength, strong swash, weak backwash
low height, short wavelength, weak swash, weak backwash
tall, short wavelength, weak swash, strong backwash
tall, long wavelength, strong swash, strong backwash
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Because the backwash is stronger than the swash, more material is dragged back down the beach than carried up it, so the beach loses sediment. Option 1 describes a constructive wave, which builds the beach up.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: The fetch of a wave is…
options: the distance it has travelled over open water
the height of the wave from trough to crest
the time the wind has blown for
the distance the swash travels up the beach
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: A long fetch means more time and distance for the wind to transfer energy to the water, so bigger waves. The UK's prevailing wind is from the south-west, which is why its south and west coasts have the biggest fetch.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines hydraulic power as the process by which…
options: sediment flung by breaking waves wears away a cliff
rocks transported by waves bump into each other and break up
sea water dissolves soluble rock such as chalk and limestone
breaking waves compress pockets of air in cracks in a cliff, and the pressure widens the crack and breaks off rock
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Option 1 is abrasion, option 2 attrition and option 3 solution. The 2025 paper asked for the term describing 'the force of waves crashing into the cliffs'.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Abrasion, also called corrasion, is…
options: the dissolving of limestone by sea water
the wearing away of cliffs by sediment flung by breaking waves
the compression of air in cracks by breaking waves
the breaking up of sediment as it bumps together in transport
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Abrasion needs sediment as its tool, which is why a beach of loose material in front of a cliff both protects the cliff by absorbing wave energy and supplies the material that grinds it.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Attrition is the process that…
options: wears transported rocks into smaller, rounder pieces as they bump into each other
wears away the base of a cliff to form a notch
dissolves chalk and limestone in sea water
moves sediment along the coast in a zigzag
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The 2019 paper used this as a distractor trap: attrition wears down the sediment, not the coast. It is the reason sediment gets smaller and rounder the further longshore drift carries it.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Which one of the following is a process of erosion in coastal areas?
options: Hydraulic power
Longshore drift
Rock fall
Slumping
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: This was 2023 Q03.1, word for word. Longshore drift is transportation; rock fall and slumping are mass movement.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines longshore drift as…
options: the movement of sediment out to sea by a strong backwash
the dropping of sediment where the sea loses energy
the zigzag movement of sediment along a shore, caused by waves arriving at an oblique angle and the backwash returning at right angles
the gradual retreat of a cliff line as it is undercut
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Because waves approach at an angle set by the prevailing wind, drift has one consistent direction along any stretch of coast. That single fact explains spits, groynes and the whole down-drift problem in coastal management.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: The four processes by which the sea transports material are…
options: abrasion, attrition, hydraulic power and solution
rockfall, landslide, mud slide and slumping
swash, backwash, longshore drift and deposition
traction, saltation, suspension and solution
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Traction rolls the largest material along the bed, saltation bounces smaller material, suspension carries fine material within the water, and solution carries dissolved material. Option 1 lists the erosion processes and option 2 the mass movement processes.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines slumping as…
options: loose saturated surface material moving rapidly downhill, sometimes almost as a fluid
rapid mass movement in which a whole segment of the cliff moves down-slope along a saturated shear-plane
the fall of individual blocks of rock from a cliff face under gravity
the downhill movement of all weathered material under gravity
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Option 1 is sliding and option 4 is mass movement in general. Slumping explains why the soft boulder clay of Holderness erodes so fast: after heavy rain a whole segment saturates and slides.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes mechanical from chemical weathering?
options: mechanical weathering happens above sea level and chemical weathering below it
mechanical weathering is caused by waves and chemical weathering by rain
mechanical weathering breaks rock up with no change in its chemical composition, whereas chemical weathering decomposes rock through a chemical change within it
mechanical weathering affects hard rock and chemical weathering affects soft rock
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Freeze-thaw is the standard example of mechanical weathering; sea water attacking chalk and limestone is the standard example of chemical weathering. Both are weathering, so neither involves removal by a moving force.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: By how much does water expand when it freezes?
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: From the school's quick-fire list. That expansion is what exerts pressure on the surrounding rock in freeze-thaw weathering, widening the crack until pieces break away — and it matters in the coastal, glacial and cold environments topics alike.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: A discordant coastline is one where…
options: hard and soft rock alternate in bands running parallel to the coast
the coast is made of a single rock type throughout
the coastline has been realigned by managed retreat
bands of hard and soft rock run at right angles to the coast, producing headlands and bays
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Option 1 describes a concordant coastline, which gives a straighter coast with coves. Swanage in Dorset is discordant, which is why Durlston Head and Ballard Point stand out between bays of clay and sand.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines a headland as…
options: a wide, gently sloping rock shelf at the base of a retreated cliff
a rocky coastal promontory made of rock that is resistant to erosion
a finger of deposited sediment extending out to sea
an isolated pillar of rock left when an arch collapses
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The definition continues that headlands lie between bays of less resistant rock where the land has been eroded back by the sea. Once formed, the headland takes the wave energy and the bay is sheltered, so it receives deposition.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: In the formation of a wave-cut platform, what forms first?
options: the gently sloping rock shelf
the collapse of the overhanging cliff
a wave-cut notch at the base of the cliff
the retreat of the cliff line inland
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The sequence is: the sea attacks a weakness at the base; hydraulic power and abrasion cut a notch; weathering weakens the cliff top; the overhang collapses under gravity; the cliff retreats; the debris is removed to leave the platform — and the process repeats.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines a wave cut platform as…
options: a rocky, level shelf at or around sea level representing the base of old, retreated cliffs
the undercut hollow at the foot of an actively eroding cliff
a beach of deposited material in front of a cliff
a bench of rock cut by a river at the base of a gorge
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The platform widens over time as the cliff retreats further, so its width is a record of how far the cliff line has moved. Kimmeridge Bay is the school's Dorset example.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Which is the correct order in the erosion of a headland?
options: arch, cave, stack, stump
stack, arch, cave, stump
stump, stack, arch, cave
cave, arch, stack, stump
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Waves attack a crack; hydraulic action, abrasion and solution widen it into a cave; continued erosion cuts the cave through to form an arch; the arch is weathered above and eroded below until it collapses, leaving a stack, which further erosion reduces to a stump.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines a stack as…
options: a wave-eroded passage cut through a small headland
an isolated pillar of rock left when the top of an arch has collapsed
a large hole in a cliff caused by waves forcing their way into cracks
a rocky promontory of resistant rock between two bays
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Option 1 is an arch, option 3 a cave and option 4 a headland. Old Harry Rocks, in chalk at Ballard Point in Dorset, is the school's named example of arches, caves and stacks.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: A stump is…
options: the notch cut at the base of an actively eroding cliff
the base of a collapsed arch left standing on the wave-cut platform
a stack that further erosion has reduced to a smaller, lower feature
a pillar of rock standing in the mouth of a cave
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: AQA's definition of a stack ends: 'over time further erosion reduces the stack to a smaller, lower stump'. It is the last stage in the sequence.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: AQA defines a beach as the zone of deposited material extending…
options: from the low water line to the limit of storm waves
from the high water line to the base of the cliff
from the low water line to the high water line
from the base of the dunes to the sea
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The beach can be divided into the foreshore and the backshore. Sandy beaches are built by constructive waves and are wide and gently sloping; pebble beaches are built by destructive waves and are steeper.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Why is marram grass so important in sand dune formation?
options: it fixes nitrogen, which fertilises the bare sand
its broad leaves trap wind-blown sand
it shades the sand, reducing evaporation
it tolerates salt spray and burial, and its long roots bind and stabilise the sand
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Stabilising the dune allows humus to accumulate and less tolerant species to colonise, which is why vegetation cover and species diversity rise from the embryo dune to the mature dune — 25% cover and 2 species against 100% cover and 22 species in the 2025 data.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Why does a spit usually have a curved end?
options: the river flowing out beside it pushes the sediment seawards
opposing winds and currents push the accumulating sediment landwards
longshore drift reverses direction twice a year
the sheltered water behind the spit silts up and forces it round
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: AQA's definition says exactly this. The other detail worth adding is that the sheltered water behind the spit becomes salt marsh, because low energy allows fine sediment to settle and vegetation to colonise.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: What happens when a spit grows all the way across a bay?
options: it is eroded away by waves refracting round the headland
it becomes a tombolo, joining the mainland to an island
it becomes a bar, and the water trapped behind it forms a lagoon
it becomes a wave-cut platform at the mouth of the bay
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Slapton Ley at Torcross is the school's named bar. A tombolo is a bar that joins the mainland to an island — Chesil Beach to the Isle of Portland.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Old Harry Rocks, the school's Dorset example of caves, arches and stacks, is formed in…
options: chalk
Purbeck Limestone
boulder clay
Kimmeridge Clay
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Chalk, at Ballard Point. Resistant rock is needed because every stage of the sequence requires the rock to hold itself up over a void. Durlston Head is the Purbeck Limestone headland and Kimmeridge Bay is the Kimmeridge Clay and Portland Limestone wave-cut platform.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: Which Dorset location does the school's case study booklet give as its wave-cut platform example?
options: Durlston Head
Swanage Bay
Studland Bay
Kimmeridge Bay
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: Kimmeridge Bay, in Kimmeridge Clay and Portland Limestone. Durlston Head is the headland, Swanage Bay the bay, and Studland Bay the beach and sand dunes.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: What does managed retreat mean?
options: building up dunes and increasing vegetation
allowing the sea to flood or erode an area of low-value land
using concrete or artificial structures to defend against natural processes
working with natural processes to restore beaches
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: This was 2024 Q03.1, with these exact options. Option 1 is dune regeneration, option 3 is hard engineering and option 4 is soft engineering. Note the words low-value — it is a deliberate decision, which is why it is called managed.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: According to the school's cost table, a sea wall costs roughly…
options: £500 per metre
£2000 per metre
£10 000 per metre
£750 per metre
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The full table: sea wall £10 000/m, rock armour £2000/m, groynes £750/m, gabions £500/m, beach nourishment £500/m, dune regeneration £20/m. A sea wall lasts 30–50 years, so the cost is spread over decades.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: What is the main drawback of building groynes?
options: by trapping sediment they deprive another area, down-drift, of new beach material
they reflect wave energy, which scours the beach in front of them
they are the most expensive form of hard engineering
they prevent beaches from being used by tourists
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: AQA's own definition includes this. The named evidence is Mappleton, where rock armour and two rock groynes removed the risk to the village but increased erosion to the south, and Hornsea, where down-drift beaches are starved of sediment.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: How long is the stretch of coastline managed under the Brighton scheme?
options: 1 km
100 km
2 km
10 km, from the River Adur to Brighton Marina
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: The scheme protects a high-value built-up area including Brighton Pier, the i360, Brighton Marina, high-value seafront property near Hove and the A259 coastal road.

06-coastal-landscapes.q: What is the annual value of tourism to the area protected by the Brighton coastal management scheme?
options: £5bn
06-coastal-landscapes.explain: £5bn a year — the figure that justifies the £11m new scheme of rock armour, a new sea wall, longer groynes and beach nourishment. £2.3bn is the value of tourism in the Lake District.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: AQA defines freeze-thaw weathering as a process that occurs when…
options: water enters cracks during the warmer day and freezes at night, expanding and exerting pressure until pieces of rock break off
meltwater freezes around loose rock and the moving ice pulls it away
rocks frozen into the base of a glacier scratch and scrape the bedrock below
ice moves in a circular motion, eroding hollows into bowl shapes
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Option 2 is plucking, option 3 abrasion and option 4 rotational slip. Freeze-thaw, also called frost-shattering, is weathering — not erosion — and the 2019 paper used that confusion as a distractor.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What percentage of visitors to the Lake District arrive by road?
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: 89%, which is why traffic congestion and air pollution in Ambleside are the dominant environmental problem, and why park and ride services such as the Honister Rambler and the Park and Sail scheme exist.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Which two landscape features does the school mat give as products of freeze-thaw weathering?
options: drumlins and erratics
corries and arêtes
scree slopes and block-fields
till plains and outwash plains
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Scree slopes are accumulations of angular shattered fragments at the base of a rock face; block-fields are areas of shattered blocks on a plateau. Both prove freeze-thaw has visible products, not just a mechanism.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Plucking is the process in which…
options: ice pushes material of all shapes and sizes ahead of it as it advances
rocks in the base of the glacier act like a giant file on the bedrock
meltwater streams sort and round material in front of the glacier
meltwater in the glacier freezes onto rocks and, as the ice moves forward, pulls out large pieces along the rock joints
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Because plucking works along joints it leaves a jagged, pitted surface — in contrast to the smooth, striated surface abrasion produces. Option 1 is bulldozing and option 2 abrasion.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What does abrasion mean?
options: rocks trapped beneath the glacier scratch and smooth the bedrock underneath
meltwater freezes beneath the ice and tears away pieces of loose rock
glacial ice moves in a circular motion causing hollows to form in the landscape
water freezes in cracks and expands, causing the rock to break down
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2024 Q05.1, with these exact options. Each distractor is the definition of something else — plucking, rotational slip and freeze-thaw weathering respectively.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Which of these is a process of glacial erosion?
options: Freeze-thaw
Plucking
Rotational slip
Transportation
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2019 Q05.4. Keep the four lists apart: erosion is abrasion and plucking; weathering is freeze-thaw; movement and transport are rotational slip and bulldozing; deposition is till and outwash.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Rotational slip is…
options: the sliding of a glacier over bedrock on a film of meltwater
the movement of ice like plastic when it is too cold to slide
the movement of ice in a circular motion, which erodes hollows and deepens them into bowl shapes
the rolling of boulders along the base of a glacier
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: It is why a corrie ends up armchair-shaped rather than simply deeper, so it belongs in every corrie answer. Option 1 is basal flow and option 2 internal deformation.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Which term describes the process where a glacier moves forward and pushes material ahead of it?
options: Plucking
Rotational slip
Abrasion
Bulldozing
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2025 Q05.1. AQA's definition is that ice pushes material of all shapes and sizes as it moves slowly forward — it is how a terminal moraine is built at the snout.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: How does a glacier move?
options: by basal flow, sliding over the bedrock on a film of meltwater, and by internal deformation, where the ice moves like plastic
only by sliding on meltwater beneath the ice
only by the weight of accumulating snow pushing it downhill
by freezing to the bedrock and then rolling forward
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Internal deformation is what happens where it is too cold for basal flow. Gravity causes the compressed ice to flow over the lip of the hollow it formed in.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What proportion of houses in the Lake District are second homes?
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: 20%, which is the clearest figure for the social impact of tourism: second homeowners can price out locals, and villages lose the permanent residents the local services depend on.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why do most UK corries face north or east?
options: the prevailing wind blows the ice in that direction
these slopes are steeper, so ice can accumulate more easily
north- and east-facing slopes are shaded, so snow survives the summer and can compress into ice
the rock on these slopes is softer and erodes faster
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: On a south-facing slope the snow melts each year, so it never accumulates and no glacier forms. East-facing slopes also collect snow blown over the ridge by the prevailing south-westerly wind.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: AQA defines till as…
options: material, chiefly sand or gravel, deposited by meltwater streams
frost-shattered debris carried on the surface of a glacier
a large boulder carried far from its source region
an unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders carried by a glacier and deposited as ground moraine over a large area
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Unsorted is the examined word: ice carries everything at once and, being solid, cannot sort by size or round the fragments. Option 1 is outwash and option 3 an erratic.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Outwash differs from till because outwash is…
options: sorted and rounded, because it is deposited by meltwater streams
angular and unsorted, because it is deposited directly by ice
found only beneath the glacier, never in front of it
made up entirely of boulders too large for meltwater to move
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Water's carrying capacity depends on particle size and velocity, so it drops the heaviest material first and carries the finest furthest, and attrition in transport rounds the fragments. That is why the 2019 data showed a sediment range of 25.3 cm on the till plain against 6.6 cm on the outwash plain.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why is the material deposited by a glacier mixed in size and shape?
options: the glacier picks up material from several different rock types
ice carries material on its surface, inside itself and at its base all at once and, being solid, cannot sort it by size
meltwater mixes the material as the glacier retreats
bulldozing crushes large boulders into smaller fragments
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2022 Q05.5. Ice has no sorting mechanism and does not round the fragments by attrition, because they are locked in place rather than knocking against one another — which is exactly what makes till unsorted and angular.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: AQA defines a corrie as…
options: a long, narrow lake found on the floor of a glaciated valley
a sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries
an armchair-shaped hollow in the mountainside formed by glacial erosion, rotational slip and freeze-thaw weathering
a river valley widened and deepened into a U-shape by a glacier
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The definition adds that this is where the valley glacier begins, and that when the ice melts it can leave a small circular lake called a tarn. Option 2 is an arête and option 4 a glacial trough.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What is tourism worth to the Lake District each year?
options: £5bn
£2.3bn and 75 000 jobs
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: That is the economic benefit to weigh against footpath erosion, boat pollution in Windermere, congestion in Ambleside and 20% second homes. Coniferous forestry is the £30m figure; £5bn is the value of tourism protected at Brighton.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why does a corrie have a lip at its downhill end?
options: the ice is thinner there so moves more slowly and erodes less, and frost-shattered rock may be deposited there
the rock at the front of the hollow is always more resistant
meltwater deposits a ridge of outwash across the exit
rotational slip lifts material up and over the front edge
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The lip is what dams the meltwater to form a tarn once the ice has gone. The lip and the tarn are the two easiest extra marks on a corrie question and are routinely left out.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: An arête is…
options: a steep pyramid-shaped summit where several corries meet
a sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries cutting back by erosion and freeze-thaw
a former river spur sliced off by a valley glacier
a tributary valley left high above the main valley floor
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Striding Edge on Helvellyn is the school's Lake District example. Option 1 is a pyramidal peak, option 3 a truncated spur and option 4 a hanging valley.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A pyramidal peak forms where…
options: two corries cut back towards each other on opposite sides of a ridge
a glacier over-deepens the floor of its trough
several corries cut back to meet at a central point, leaving a steep pyramid
freeze-thaw weathering shatters a summit into angular blocks
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Two corries back to back give an arête; three or more meeting at a point give a pyramidal peak. Both are produced by the same back-wall retreat that forms the corries themselves.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why does a glacier produce a U-shaped valley where a river produces a V-shaped one?
options: glacial ice is denser than water, so it erodes downwards more strongly
glaciers only occupy valleys that were already wide
rivers erode in summer only, whereas glaciers erode all year
the ice fills the whole valley and is rigid, so it erodes the sides as well as the floor and cannot flow around obstacles
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: That one sentence explains the U-shape, the truncated spurs and the straightening of the valley at once. A river occupies only a narrow channel, so it erodes downwards and flows round obstacles, leaving interlocking spurs.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A truncated spur is…
options: a former river valley spur which has been sliced off by a valley glacier, forming cliff-like edges
a ridge of till deposited along the side of a glacier
an isolated hill of rock left standing in the middle of a glacial trough
the steep back wall of a corrie after the ice has melted
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Because the rigid ice filled the valley it could not flow around the interlocking spurs of the old river valley, so it cut straight through them.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A hanging valley is…
options: a valley dammed by a terminal moraine so that it holds a lake
a tributary valley eroded much less than the main valley, left high above its floor and often the site of a waterfall
a valley whose floor has been over-deepened into a ribbon lake
the upper part of a glacial trough above the former snow line
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: AQA's definition adds that it was too cold and high up for ice to move easily, so it was not eroded as much as the lower main valley — hence the waterfall crashing several hundred metres to the main valley floor.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A ribbon lake is a long, narrow lake formed where…
options: a terminal moraine dams the mouth of a glacial trough
meltwater ponds behind an outwash plain
the glacier had more erosive power, so the valley floor was over-deepened
two glaciers merged and their medial moraine blocked the valley
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: AQA gives three reasons the glacier might have had more erosive power there: softer rock, a temporarily steeper valley gradient, or a tributary glacier joining and adding ice. Ullswater is the school's Lake District example and Llyn Ogwen was the 2023 paper's.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A medial moraine forms where…
options: the glacier snout bulldozes material across the valley at its furthest advance
freeze-thaw debris falls onto the edge of a glacier from the valley sides
basal material is released as a sheet across the valley floor
a tributary glacier joins the main glacier and their two adjoining lateral moraines merge into one central ridge
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Option 1 is a terminal moraine, option 2 a lateral moraine and option 3 ground moraine. All four are unsorted till, because ice does not sort or round its load.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A terminal moraine marks…
options: the furthest point the glacier snout reached, as a ridge of unsorted till across the valley
the boundary between the till plain and the outwash plain at the valley sides
the line along which two glaciers merged
the upper limit of ice in the valley
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The snout bulldozes material forward by the sheer weight of the ice, and melting at the point of maximum advance releases it as a ridge. Beyond it, meltwater streams build the sorted, rounded outwash plain.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Which description of a drumlin's shape is correct?
options: a rounded hill or bump of till with no clear orientation
elongated or oval, with a steep blunt end facing up-ice and a long tapering tail down-ice
a sharp conical mound of sorted sand and gravel
a long low ridge running across the direction of ice flow
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The school's feedback lesson states that a 'hill' or 'bump' does not refer to the correct shape. The long axis is parallel to the former direction of ice, which is why drumlins occur in aligned swarms — basket-of-eggs topography.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What is the name given to a large boulder transported and deposited by glaciers in areas with a different rock type?
options: Moraine
Outwash
Erratic
Till
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2023 Q05.1. The giveaway in the stem is 'a different rock type' — because its rock does not match the local bedrock, an erratic records the direction the ice came from.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example of which landform?
options: a corrie
a ribbon lake
a drumlin
an arête
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The school's Lake District set is: arête Striding Edge, ribbon lake Ullswater, corrie Blea Water, U-shaped valley Langdale (all erosion), and drumlins at Swindale (deposition).

07-glacial-landscapes.q: How many tourists visit the Lake District each year?
options: 18 million
1.8 million
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: 18 million, against just 40 000 local people — roughly 450 visitors per resident, which is the ratio that explains footpath erosion, congestion and the second-home problem. The school's model answer quotes 18.4 million.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: The Honister Slate Mine in the Lake District is significant because it…
options: was closed by the National Park authority to protect the landscape
combines working quarrying with tourism, offering climbing and a 1 km zip-wire
is the site of the Fix the Fells footpath repair scheme
imposes a 10 knot speed limit to protect the lake
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: It shows development and conservation are not always opposed — which is the direct comparison for the 2023 question on the contested zip wire proposed across the Thirlmere Valley. The 10 knot limit applies to boats on Lake Windermere.
